stature.source: typical and tall: the drafter's estimate for the Sierra (the Gymnosperm Database gives the species to 55 m, often dwarfed in snowy subalpine sites); record: 59.1 m, Olympic National Park, 1998 (Gymnosperm Database, which warns the method may overestimate); read 2026-11-04

targets.from: judgement values from the drafter's reading of the sources and knowledge of the species (2026-11-04), no photographs measured; to be replaced by photo measurements: a dense, narrow cone with drooping branch tips and a nodding leader, live branches to the ground; dark blue-green

old-growth.note: an old tree of a snowy north slope: a dark furrowed trunk, branches drooping like skirts, the tip still nodding; often bent at the base by snow creep

description: A graceful hemlock of the snowiest high slopes, 10-30 m here, with a narrow cone of drooping branches, a limp leader that nods over at the very top, and short blue-green needles that stand out all around the twigs like little stars. It grows on cool, north-facing slopes and in cirque basins near timberline, about 2400-3200 m, where snow lies into July, and at its highest goes down to a low, bent shrub.

season_notes.winter: Evergreen and deep in snow; the drooping limbs shed it and young trees lie pressed flat under it.
season_notes.spring: Purple pollen cones and small purple seed cones in June-July as the snow melts off the slope.
season_notes.summer: Small cones, 3-7 cm, hang at the branch tips and turn from purple to brown.
season_notes.fall: Cones open and release tiny winged seeds onto the early snow.

range.where: the snowiest north slopes and cirque basins near timberline: Gaylor Lakes, Tioga Pass, Mount Hoffmann, Cathedral Lakes

notes: The nodding leader is the field mark (John Muir's favourite tree), and the generator has no way to bend the top few metres of the stem over; a reviewer may try a variant 'set' on the leader. Its needles radiate all round the twig rather than in two ranks, cones are small and hanging (Douglas-fir's are too, but longer and bracted). Bark dark grey to reddish-brown, deeply furrowed on larger stems (Gymnosperm Database). The deer browse line is a guess (little forage value); nothing in the animal library depends on it, though chickadees, crossbills and sooty grouse do. Sierra elevations: the Gymnosperm Database gives 2750-3050 m for the southern Sierra; the central Sierra belt is lower and is the drafter's knowledge.
